title: Israel Provoked to Jealousy
english: …insisting that the nations were not called for this reason, that Israel, having stumbled against Christ as against a stone (Romans 9:32–33), should fall away altogether from its hope in God, but rather so that, moved to jealousy by those who had been received beyond all expectation (Romans 11:11), they might choose to unlearn their baser ways, think better than before, and so receive the Redeemer.

A short example will make the point. Children who are small and not yet grown sometimes fall into the sulks that suit those who are still infants. Then they run a little way off from father or mother, pour tears from their eyes for no real cause, and grieve their parents not a little; for the law of natural affection brings them to this. And then the parents, skilfully drawing them away from their pettiness and childish folly, simply catch up any child who happens to be near and give it the marks of their own affection, so making their own child jealous and, as it were, provoking it to turn back and love them. Something of this kind, as I think, is what the inspired Paul said had been done, since he does not allow anyone to despair of Israel, though it has stumbled.

“Now if their trespass means riches for the world” (Romans 11:12). For if, he says, the world has been enriched with closeness to God because Israel stumbled, and the nations were received because Israel lacked a right mind, what then would their acceptance be, if not very nearly the undoing of death and life from the dead?

“If somehow I may make my flesh jealous” (Romans 11:14). So he draws the believers from the nations and from the Jews into one mind and peace, so that they may not be puffed up, but may offer their thanks to God, who freely granted the forgiveness of their trespasses and bore no grudge. He says that he glorifies his own ministry (Romans 11:13), not from a desire for empty glory, but, he says, “so that I may make my flesh jealous.” Here again he calls Israel his own flesh, that is, his kin according to the flesh. It is much as if he were to say: “I declare my apostleship to be glorious, worthy, and most dear to God, and most needful to all who live under the sun, not so that I might be seen crowning my own head with empty honours and outlandish boasting, but so that I might save my own kin according to the flesh.” He all but pricks them with jealousy as with a goad, and rouses them to resolve that they must be justified by the grace that comes through Christ.

“For if their rejection means the reconciliation of the world, what will their acceptance mean but life from the dead?” (Romans 11:15). Since, then, there was no way to praise Israel for its faith or its conduct, he turned to the reasoning of the economy, and says that their unbelief has become for the world the means of its closeness to God. He tries to say that by the very things in which they stumbled they have perhaps even become benefactors of the world; and so he crowns the Jews, as it were, though they have fallen and lie on the ground. For he says that their acceptance is life from the dead, if indeed it is true that their rejection has become the reconciliation of the world.

title: The Fullness of the Nations and All Israel
english: …was constructed by the apostle. For he sets Israel right, since it had fallen short of what was fitting, and he urges it toward what is to its profit, and to lay claim to its own root through faith in Christ. He also says that those from the nations have been honoured by God, and he urges them to stand firm in faith and godliness: for if you remain so, you remain a noble branch of the holy root; but if you disobey, you too will be outside the root (Romans 11:16–22).

“Until the fullness of the nations has come in; and so all Israel will be saved” (Romans 11:25–26). Look again at this and consider it closely. He said that the fullness of the nations would come in and all Israel would be saved. But suppose someone chose to answer this: “Yet many of the nations have died in unbelief; how, then, has the fullness of the nations come in? Nor will all Israel be saved, if it is true that the Jews will receive the son of lawlessness (2 Thessalonians 2:3), having cast away their love for Christ. For He Himself said this: ‘I have come in My Father’s name, and you do not receive Me; if another comes in his own name, him you will receive’ (John 5:43). And the most wise Paul says: ‘Because they did not receive the love of the truth so as to be saved, therefore God sends them a working of error, so that they believe the lie’ (2 Thessalonians 2:10–11).”

What, then, shall we say to this? We say that, since God has set the grace that comes through faith before all without stint and shuts out no one at all, how has the fullness of the nations not come in, as far as the mind and purpose of the One who called is concerned? For if some have slipped aside of their own will and missed the gift, we shall not on that account find the word of Scripture to be false. For though they were free to share in the gifts once given, why did they choose of their own will to fall away? So, as far as the gentleness and love for mankind of the One who called is concerned, the fullness of the nations has come in, and all Israel too has been saved. But since they have become unbending, for that reason he says that a hardening has come upon them in part (Romans 11:25).

“As it is written: ‘The Deliverer will come from Zion’” (Romans 11:26; Isaiah 59:20). He confirms the hope that even rejected Israel is to be saved in due time, by setting out a sacred oracle. For Israel will be saved in due time, called last, after the calling of those from the nations.

“Enemies for your sake” (Romans 11:28). As far as the preaching of the gospel is concerned, they have become enemies, for they stumbled through their impiety toward Christ. But because of the nobility of the fathers, who were honoured as holy and dear to God, they may be reckoned beloved for the fathers’ sake. Yet they have become enemies so that a cause of jealousy might be set before those who disbelieved.

“For just as you once disobeyed God,” and so on (Romans 11:30). He shows that the charges against both are equal, and that those from the nations and Israel alike have been healed by one grace. For Israel was called in its time through Moses and rescued from its misery in Egypt; but the worshippers of demons, that is, the nations,…

title: Mercy on All, and Foods Clean by Nature
english: …whom we may understand as signified by the Egyptians, for a time disobeyed the mercy shown to those of Israel. For they did not believe the divine signs worked through Moses; they would not know the God of the Hebrews. The people of the Jews was sent out, though barely, to offer sacrifice in the wilderness, while the Egyptians held fast to their ancient error. But now they have received mercy, since Israel has stumbled; and Israel in turn has disobeyed the mercy shown to the nations, so that it too may receive mercy in due time (Romans 11:30–31).

So, as I said, the charges against both are equal, and both alike have needed the help of the One who shows compassion. And he says that all have been shut up in disobedience by God, so that He may have mercy on all (Romans 11:32). Yet we shall by no means reckon it the work of the divine will that some disobeyed, so that, having fallen into this, they might also be pitied. Rather, He shut them up in disobedience by showing them to be liable to the charges of disobedience, and convicted, as it were, by the facts themselves; so that they had come at last to such misfortune that they all but stood in need of pity and mercy.

“I know and am persuaded in the Lord Jesus,” and so on (Romans 14:14). “I know and am persuaded,” he says, “in the Lord Jesus that nothing is common of itself,” and the rest. The witness who firmly declares that he knows and is persuaded is trustworthy. He adds “in the Lord Jesus” so that the truth may be established still more firmly, and so that his hearers may follow in faith without any hesitation. No doubt he remembers that Christ said, “It is not what goes into the mouth that defiles a man” (Matthew 15:11), and that all food passes into the stomach and is sent out into the drain (Matthew 15:17); this is its nature and its use. So, as far as their own nature goes, nothing that serves as food is common or profane, “for it is made holy by the word of God and prayer” (1 Timothy 4:5).

And we remember that when God had brought all things into being, He saw, it says, that they were “very good” (Genesis 1:31), and He blessed them (Genesis 1:22). Since God praised and indeed blessed His own creatures, who would dare to say that they cause defilement and profanation, and not thereby bring a charge against the very One who brought them into being? So nothing that has been made is common by nature at all. But if someone should think that anything is common, for that very reason he himself has been made common, and has caught the profanation, as it were, in his own judgment. For all things are clean (Romans 14:20); what makes the unbeliever common is his little faith about certain things, and not at all the things themselves that he has supposed to be common.

For just as, to those mature in mind, there is one God by nature and no other beside Him, and an idol is nothing in the world (1 Corinthians 8:4), and food offered to idols is counted as nothing (for how could one who does not know an idol know food offered to idols?), while to those who think there are many gods there will certainly be such a thing as food offered to idols (1 Corinthians 8:5–7), so, for those who have believed, the things that come from God are unprofaned and clean, and nothing at all is common by nature, and what is left wholly free is…
